summary: The City Council unanimously voted on September 15, 2023 to increase funding for local emergency services, following a review by the fire and police chiefs that identified outdated equipment, vehicle shortages and training needs. The money will go to equipment, infrastructure and training, and is funded by a mix of budget reallocation, a state grant and a sales tax increase. Officials and residents voiced support, and analysts expect faster response times and better staff retention.
one_line: The City Council unanimously approved increased emergency services funding on September 15, 2023 for equipment, infrastructure and training, paid by reallocation, a state grant and sales tax.
key_facts: The City Council unanimously voted to increase funding for local emergency services on September 15, 2023, at its monthly meeting.
Fire Chief Hernandez and Chief of Police Maria Vasquez presented a review citing outdated equipment, a shortage of emergency vehicles, and the need for more first responder training.
City Treasurer Rebecca O'Neill submitted the budget proposal, which targets three areas: emergency response equipment, infrastructure renovation, and first responder training programs.
Fire stations will replace aging fire trucks and ambulances and acquire new Jaws of Life tools and thermal imaging cameras.
The City Police Department will receive funds to expand its fleet of patrol cars and adopt new technology to improve communication and response times.
Training courses will include advanced life support, hazardous materials handling, cybercrime prevention, and community policing strategies for paramedics, EMTs, firefighters and police officers.

Funding sources are a small reallocation of existing budget funds, a state emergency grant secured earlier in the fiscal year, and a marginal city sales tax increase previously approved for emergency services.
The use of taxation generated some debate among council members and the public, but local surveys showed strong public support for improving emergency response.
Councilmember John Lee said "Investing in our emergency services is not a matter of debate; it's a necessity for safeguarding our community."
Councilmember Susan Cho backed the proposal, saying it would improve efficacy and instill greater public confidence.
Community leader and small business owner Maria Gonzales endorsed the increase during public commentary, saying "Our emergency teams are our lifeline."
An initial assessment suggests emergency call response times could fall by up to two minutes.
The funding is also expected to help retain and attract qualified emergency personnel through competitive compensation, equipment and training.
The City Council pledged close oversight, transparency and regular progress reporting during implementation.
